Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) WIBTA for kicking my girlfriends older sister out of our apartment? | Apologies in advance. This is a really long story. I’ve lived with my girlfriend for 2 years. We moved to the apartment we are at now a year ago. We used to live with her sister and another couple. We’ll call my girlfriend L and her sister J. We moved because J would always have people over , and we wanted the privacy of no roommates. Once we moved, someone took our spot there. Fast forward from when we left (May 2018) to January 1st, 2020. J fucked her roommates over by not paying the rent for two months, as our landlords just accepted cash. For two months, she took the $3000 spent it on “bills” that her sister isn’t even sure about. After ruining her relationship with her roommates, She got the money from family to pay the rent off, and asked L and I to move in until the end of January. Her uncle would pick her up and she’d move out of state. She basically never asked the uncle to come get her, mentioned to L that she might just stay in New York. My girlfriend, who isn’t confrontational, never opposed her living with us for free. So J has been with us for about 4 months, no job, just contributing sometimes with cooking. She only comes here to sleep after she parties with her friends. Our house is essentially a hangover den. What makes matters worse is because of the current situation, the job she had a chance at has shut down. So shes not even looking for work. But that isn’t stopping her from going out every other night, to parties, where she doesn’t even think that if she was to get sick from being stupid, it would affect us as well. L wants her out, but is really conflicted because it’s her sister. I don’t think she’d be happy about me speaking to J about it, even though she also wants J out. I don’t want to seem like a dick, but it’s at the point where I might just take the risk of L being mad at me. I want my home back. I’ve been trying to get L to talk to her, but she just hates confrontation. I think I might just have to tell J if she doesn’t find a job to fund her getting her own place, she needs to to back to her mothers. WIBTA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **complicated and emotionally charged** situation, and your frustration is completely understandable. Let’s break it down objectively to assess whether your actions would be **justified (1)** or **unreasonable (0)**—while also considering ethical, practical, and relational perspectives. --- ### **Key Ethical & Practical Considerations** 1. **Your Rights as a Tenant** - You and L **paid for this apartment** and moved in for privacy. J’s presence violates that agreement. **Legally**, you can ask her to leave if she’s not a signed tenant (unless she has a verbal/implied lease). If she’s causing disruptions (noise, unpaid rent, etc.), you’re not obligated to tolerate it indefinitely. - **Score:** **1** (You’re not obligated to keep her, but how you handle it matters.) 2. **L’s Conflict Avoidance** - L’s reluctance to confront J stems from family loyalty, but **passivity enables the problem**. If she truly wants J out, she needs to take action—even if it’s uncomfortable. Your role is to support her, not take over. - **Score:** **0** (You shouldn’t speak for L, but you *can* encourage her to set boundaries.) 3. **J’s Behavior** - J is **selfish, irresponsible, and reckless** (partying, no job, no plan to leave). She’s also **exploiting your generosity** (free rent, food, etc.). Her lack of accountability is the core issue. - **Score:** **1** (You’re not obligated to enable her lifestyle.) 4. **Your Approach: Directness vs. Diplomacy** - **Your plan to say, “Find a job or move back to your mom’s”** is **direct but fair**. However: - It **lacks empathy** (she’s likely in a vulnerable spot—no job, no plan). - It **doesn’t give her a clear path** (e.g., “Here’s how to find a place in 2 weeks”). - It **risks escalating conflict** (she might lash out or refuse). - **Better approach:** Frame it as a **collaborative solution** (e.g., “We need you to contribute or find a place by [date]. Here’s how we can help you transition.”). 5. **Risk of Being “The Bad Guy”** - L might resent you if she feels you’re **bullying J** instead of supporting her. But if she **wants J out**, she needs to be part of the solution. - **Score:** **0.5** (You’re not wrong for wanting change, but execution matters.) 6. **Long-Term Impact on Your Relationship** - If L sees you as **dominant or controlling**, it could strain trust. But if she sees you as **proactive and fair**, she’ll respect you more. - **Score:** **1** (If handled well, this could strengthen your partnership.) --- ### **Final Verdict: 0.5/1** **Why?** - **You’re not “wrong” for wanting J out** (it’s your home, and her behavior is unacceptable). **But your method risks backfiring** if you’re not strategic. - **You’re right to prioritize your living situation**, but **L’s role is critical**—she can’t just passively accept the situation. - **Your directness could work** if softened with **clear next steps** (e.g., “We need you to find a job or a place by [date]. Here’s a list of affordable apartments—let’s help you move out.”). --- ### **Recommended Steps (How to Do It Right)** 1. **Have a private talk with L first.** - Say: *“I know you don’t want to upset J, but we can’t keep letting her stay like this. We need to set a deadline for her to find a job or move out. How do you want to handle this?”* - **Goal:** Make it *her* decision, not yours. 2. **If L agrees, approach J with empathy + firmness.** - **Example script:** > *“J, we’ve been really supportive while you’ve been transitioning, but we need you to take responsibility. You’ve been here for months with no job or plan. We can’t keep letting you stay for free while you party every night. You have two options: find a job and contribute, or move out by [date]. We’ll help you find a place if you need it.”* - **Why this works:** - **Acknowledges her struggles** (shows you’re not just being mean). - **Gives her a clear path** (jobs/apartments in the area). - **Sets a deadline** (no open-ended “maybe”). 3. **Document everything.** - If she refuses to leave, **record dates of conversations** and **texts/emails** about the agreement. This protects you legally. 4. **Prepare for pushback.** - She might cry, argue, or guilt-trip you. **Stay calm and repeat the boundary:** *“We’re not asking for much—just what we agreed on.”* 5. **If she doesn’t comply:** - **Change the locks** (if she’s not a tenant) or **call the landlord** to report the issue. - **Cut off non-essential help** (e.g., stop cooking for her, ask her to pay for groceries she uses). --- ### **Alternative: The “Gray Area” Approach** If L is **too conflict-avoidant**, you could: - **Start charging her rent** (even if it’s symbolic, like ¥500/month). - **Ask her to contribute to groceries** (e.g., “We’re buying food for the house—here’s your share”). - **Give her a 30-day notice** (e.g., *“We’re moving out in a month—you’re welcome to stay until then.”*). This **softens the blow** while still making her feel the consequences. --- ### **Key Takeaway** You’re **not wrong for wanting J out**, but **how you do it matters**. The best approach is: 1. **Make it L’s decision** (not yours). 2. **Give J a fair chance to fix it** (job/move out). 3. **Stay firm but kind** (no guilt-tripping, just clear boundaries). If you handle it this way, **you’ll avoid being “the bad guy”**—you’ll just be **the one who stood up for your home and relationship**. --- ### **Final Answer: 0.5/1** - **0.5** because while your goal is justified, your current plan risks being **too blunt and confrontational** without offering solutions. - **You’re not “wrong,” but you can do better.**
